problemSolved: A browser, app, or external API consumer from outside the cluster — the origin of every inbound request the hosted cluster must serve.
interactions: Sends HTTPS requests to the cluster's public Route hostname resolved by external DNS.

For control-plane / API traffic the Shared Ingress Proxy only SNI-routes the TLS connection (passthrough) and TLS terminates at the guest kube-apiserver; for *.apps application traffic TLS is terminated by the guest cluster's own Ingress Router.
explorationCommands:
# Simulate a request from outside the cluster
curl -v https://<route-hostname>/api/endpoint

problemSolved: The single control-plane factory: it turns every HostedCluster request into a running, hosted control plane.
interactions: Runs as one cluster-wide singleton Deployment in the management cluster's 'hypershift' namespace — it manages every HostedCluster, not one instance per guest.
Watches HostedCluster and NodePool custom resources in the management API Server.
Creates the dedicated HCP namespace per hosted cluster and deploys the control-plane-operator into it.
Runs the NodePool controller, translating NodePools into Cluster API objects and delegating to the infrastructure provider (KubeVirt/CAPK, AWS, Azure, bare-metal Agent).
explorationCommands:
# Check HyperShift operator status
oc get pods -n hypershift

# List all HostedClusters
oc get hostedcluster -A

# View a HostedCluster spec
oc get hostedcluster <name> -n <namespace> -o yaml

problemSolved: The one object an admin writes to ask OpenShift for a whole guest control plane.
interactions: Authored by the platform admin and stored in the management API Server.
Reconciled by the HyperShift Operator, which derives the HCP namespace and a HostedControlPlane CR from it.
Surfaces overall control-plane availability and version in its status.
Declares the desired control plane: release image, networking, platform (KubeVirt here), and publishing strategy.
explorationCommands:
# List HostedClusters
oc get hostedcluster -A

# Inspect a HostedCluster's conditions
oc get hostedcluster <name> -n clusters -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions}'

problemSolved: The only knob for guest workers — declaring one scales the hosted cluster's worker nodes up or down.
interactions: Authored by the platform admin alongside the HostedCluster, stored in the management API Server.
Reconciled by the HyperShift Operator's NodePool controller into Cluster API objects (Cluster, MachineDeployment).
Scaling or changing the NodePool replica count adds or removes guest worker VMIs.
The hosted-cluster analogue of a MachineSet: it declares the replica count, instance type / VM template, and upgrade strategy for the workers.
There is no standalone Machine API in the guest; all worker scaling flows through NodePools.
explorationCommands:
# List NodePools for a hosted cluster
oc get nodepool -n clusters

# Scale a NodePool
oc scale nodepool <name> -n clusters --replicas=3

# Inspect NodePool status
oc get nodepool <name> -n clusters -o yaml

problemSolved: Keeps the guest cluster pinned at its intended OpenShift version — nothing else owns guest upgrades.
interactions: Reads the ClusterVersion CR to determine target version.
Applies manifests from the release image to the guest API Server.
Monitors ClusterOperator status and blocks upgrades when operators are degraded.
explorationCommands:
# View cluster version and upgrade status
oc get clusterversion

# Check cluster operator conditions
oc get clusteroperators

# View CVO logs
oc logs -n <hcp-namespace> deployment/cluster-version-operator --tail=50

problemSolved: The per-guest operator that actually builds this hosted cluster's control-plane components into existence.
interactions: Reconciles the HostedControlPlane CR created by the HyperShift Operator.
Creates and manages the Deployments/StatefulSets for every guest control-plane component in the HCP namespace.
Wires up certificates, kubeconfigs, and service endpoints between the components.

While the HyperShift Operator is one cluster-wide controller, the CPO is deployed per HCP namespace to reconcile this guest's own etcd, API server, OAuth, Konnectivity, Ignition, and OVN control plane.
explorationCommands:
# Check the control-plane-operator pod
oc get pods -n <hcp-namespace> -l app=control-plane-operator

# View CPO logs
oc logs -n <hcp-namespace> deployment/control-plane-operator --tail=50

# Inspect the HostedControlPlane it reconciles
oc get hostedcontrolplane -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

problemSolved: Drives the generic machine lifecycle that ultimately provisions guest worker nodes.
interactions: Reconciles Cluster API Machine/MachineSet/MachineDeployment objects in the HCP namespace.
Delegates infrastructure creation to the platform provider (cluster-api-provider-kubevirt here).
Reports Machine status (provisioning, running, deleting) back up to the NodePool controller.
explorationCommands:
# Check the CAPI manager pod
oc get pods -n <hcp-namespace> -l control-plane=capi-controller-manager

# List the Machines for this hosted cluster
oc get machines.cluster.x-k8s.io -n <hcp-namespace>

# View MachineDeployment status
oc get machinedeployment -n <hcp-namespace>

problemSolved: Bridges generic Cluster API machines to real KubeVirt VMs that become guest worker nodes.
interactions: Watches KubevirtMachine objects produced by the CAPI manager.
Creates and manages KubeVirt VirtualMachine / VirtualMachineInstance objects in the HCP namespace.
Reports VM readiness and node addresses back to Cluster API.
explorationCommands:
# Check the CAPK provider pod
oc get pods -n <hcp-namespace> -l control-plane=capi-kubevirt-controller-manager

# List the VirtualMachines backing the worker nodes
oc get vm -n <hcp-namespace>

# Inspect a KubevirtMachine
oc get kubevirtmachine -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

problemSolved: The front door to the guest cluster — every kubectl/oc command and controller talks to it.
interactions: Exposes the guest cluster's API on a dedicated Service port.
Persists objects to the guest Etcd StatefulSet Pod in the same namespace — a regular Pod, not a static pod.
Notifies guest controllers (scheduler, controller-manager) of state changes via watch events.
Runs as a Pod in the management cluster (not inside a guest VM), handling authentication, authorization, and admission for all guest API traffic.
explorationCommands:
# Get guest API server URL
oc get hostedcluster <name> -n <ns> -o jsonpath='{.status.controlPlaneEndpoint}'

# Check guest API server health
curl -k https://<guest-api-endpoint>/healthz

# View API server logs
oc logs -n <hcp-namespace> deployment/kube-apiserver --tail=50

problemSolved: Issues the tokens that authenticate users to the guest cluster.
interactions: Validates identity provider credentials and issues OAuth tokens.
Integrates with the Guest API Server for RBAC enforcement.
Persists OAuth access/authorize tokens as objects in the guest cluster's own etcd (the guest Etcd StatefulSet), not the management cluster's etcd.
Runs as a Pod in the management cluster, isolated from the guest node infrastructure.
explorationCommands:
# View OAuth server logs
oc logs -n <hcp-namespace> deployment/oauth-server --tail=50

# Check OAuth routes on the guest cluster
oc get route oauth-openshift -n openshift-authentication

problemSolved: Runs the core Kubernetes control loops that keep the guest cluster reconciled to desired state.
interactions: Watches the Guest API Server for resource events.
Manages ReplicaSet scaling, Endpoint slice population, and node health.
Writes status updates back to the Guest API Server.
Hosts the NodeLifecycle, Endpoint, Deployment and other controllers in a single Pod in the management cluster.
explorationCommands:
# View controller manager logs
oc logs -n <hcp-namespace> deployment/kube-controller-manager --tail=50

# Check controller leases
oc get lease -n kube-system

problemSolved: Decides which guest worker node each pending guest Pod runs on.
interactions: Watches Guest API Server for pending Pods.
Evaluates guest node capacity reported by guest kubelet via guest API Server.
Writes binding objects back to the Guest API Server to finalize scheduling.
explorationCommands:
# View scheduler logs
oc logs -n <hcp-namespace> deployment/kube-scheduler --tail=50

# Inspect scheduling events for a guest pod
oc describe pod <pod-name> -n <ns> | grep -A5 Events

problemSolved: The guest cluster's source of truth — it persists every object the guest API server serves.
interactions: Receives reads and writes exclusively from the Guest API Server.
Replicates data across the StatefulSet's etcd members via the Raft consensus protocol.
The control-plane-operator manages etcd member lifecycle and backups for this hosted cluster.
Runs as a StatefulSet Pod inside the guest's HCP namespace, not a static pod (static pods only exist on kubelet-managed nodes).
explorationCommands:
# Check etcd health
oc exec -n <hcp-namespace> etcd-0 -- etcdctl endpoint health

# List etcd members
oc exec -n <hcp-namespace> etcd-0 -- etcdctl member list

# Confirm etcd is a StatefulSet, not a static pod
oc get statefulset etcd -n <hcp-namespace>

problemSolved: The single TLS front door that SNI-routes inbound API traffic to the right guest's control plane.
interactions: Fronts the guest control-plane endpoints (kube-apiserver :6443, oauth-openshift, konnectivity, ignition-server) and routes inbound TLS to them by SNI / hostname.
Selected by the Shared Ingress LoadBalancer Service, which gives it a single external VIP shared across hosted clusters.
Forwards to the per-guest control-plane Services in the HCP namespace — traffic terminates in the management control plane and never enters a guest worker VM.
Carries control-plane / API ingress only — never the guest's *.apps application traffic, which uses the guest cluster's own ingress router.
explorationCommands:
# Check the shared ingress proxy pods
oc get pods -n hypershift-sharedingress

# View the HAProxy SNI routing config
oc exec -n hypershift-sharedingress <proxy-pod> -- cat /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg | head -60

# List the per-guest control-plane Services it fronts
oc get svc -n <hcp-namespace> kube-apiserver oauth-openshift konnectivity-server ignition-server

linuxPrimitive: MetalLB L2 VIP (ARP/NDP) → OVN LB flows
problemSolved: Gives the hosted clusters' control-plane endpoints one stable external IP to dial.
interactions: Selects the Shared Ingress Proxy Pods and publishes their endpoints behind one external control-plane VIP.
MetalLB (L2 mode) advertises the VIP via gratuitous ARP/NDP from a single elected speaker node.
OVN-Kubernetes programs load-balancer flows that DNAT the VIP to a healthy proxy Pod (OVN-K replaces kube-proxy, so there is no kube-proxy in this datapath).
Application (*.apps wildcard Route) traffic does not use this VIP — it enters via the Apps Ingress LoadBalancer instead.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect the LoadBalancer service and its assigned external IP
oc get svc -n hypershift-sharedingress -o wide

# Check which node MetalLB is advertising the VIP from
oc logs -n metallb-system -l component=speaker --tail=50 | grep announcing

# View the MetalLB L2 advertisement / address pool
oc get l2advertisement,ipaddresspool -n metallb-system

problemSolved: The bare-metal entry point that carries the guest's *.apps application traffic into the worker VMs.
interactions: Created and reconciled by the kubevirt cloud provider (Cloud Controller Manager) to mirror the guest cluster's router-default LoadBalancer Service.
Selects the virt-launcher Pods that host the guest worker VMIs and forwards to the NodePort where the in-VM OpenShift Ingress Router listens.
MetalLB (L2 mode) advertises its external VIP via ARP/NDP; the hosted cluster's *.apps wildcard DNS resolves here.
Does NOT serve the guest API / OAuth / Konnectivity / Ignition endpoints — those ride the Shared Ingress Proxy.
explorationCommands:
# Find the infra LoadBalancer the kubevirt CCM created for the guest router
oc get svc -n <hcp-namespace> -l kubevirt.io/cluster-name -o wide

# Confirm the matching router-default LB inside the guest cluster
oc get svc router-default -n openshift-ingress -o wide --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# See which node MetalLB advertises the VIP from
oc logs -n metallb-system -l component=speaker --tail=50 | grep announcing

problemSolved: Translates the guest cluster's Services and NetworkPolicies into the logical network OVN enforces.
interactions: Watches the Guest API Server for Pod, Service, and NetworkPolicy events.
Writes to the OVN Northbound Database to update logical switch topology.
Northbound DB is synced to the OVN Southbound DB and pushed to each node's OVN controller.
Runs as a Pod in the management cluster, programming the OVN Northbound DB for the guest.
explorationCommands:
# View OVN control-plane logs
oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes deployment/ovnkube-control-plane --tail=50

# Inspect logical switches
ovn-nbctl show

# Check OVN southbound flows
ovn-sbctl lflow-list | head -30

problemSolved: The guest cluster's bridge to infrastructure — it realises LoadBalancers and node addresses that have no cloud behind them.
interactions: Watches Node objects in the guest cluster for ProviderID fields.
Calls cloud provider APIs to provision or update load balancers for LoadBalancer-type Services.
Reports cloud-specific node metadata back to the Guest API Server.
explorationCommands:
# Check CCM logs
oc logs -n <hcp-namespace> deployment/cloud-controller-manager --tail=50

# List cloud provider resources
oc get nodes -o wide

problemSolved: Lets the guest API server reach node kubelets (exec, logs, port-forward) across a network it can't route to directly.
interactions: Maintains persistent tunnels from the bare metal cluster to Konnectivity Agents on each guest worker node.
Proxies API Server → kubelet calls (exec, logs, port-forward) through the tunnel.
Used by the Guest API Server for all node-targeted traffic.
explorationCommands:
# Check konnectivity server
oc logs -n <hcp-namespace> deployment/konnectivity-server --tail=50

# Verify tunnel health
oc get pods -n <hcp-namespace> -l app=konnectivity-server

problemSolved: Hands each booting worker node the config it needs to join the guest cluster — enabling zero-touch provisioning.
interactions: Provides a TLS-secured endpoint serving node-specific Ignition configs.
Injects the kubelet bootstrap credentials and the machine config (systemd units, kubelet config, pull secrets, certificates) the node applies on first boot.
Called once per node boot; after that, the node's kubelet manages its own certs.
explorationCommands:
# Check ignition server
oc get pods -n <hcp-namespace> -l app=ignition-server

# View ignition config for a node (requires admin certs)
curl -k https://<ignition-endpoint>/ignition

problemSolved: Collects the guest cluster's metrics and alerts — on the guest's own nodes, like any OpenShift cluster.
interactions: Scrapes metrics endpoints on guest cluster Pods and nodes from within the guest cluster.
Stores time-series data in a Thanos-backed Prometheus instance running on guest nodes.
Exposes metrics via the guest cluster's OpenShift monitoring console.
Runs as applications on the guest worker nodes (inside the VMs), not in the management control-plane namespace.
explorationCommands:
# Check monitoring stack (from the guest cluster)
oc get pods -n openshift-monitoring --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Query Prometheus directly
oc exec -n openshift-monitoring prometheus-k8s-0 --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig> -- promtool query instant http://localhost:9090 'up'

runtimeForm: systemd unit · bare metal master node
problemSolved: The agent that runs the management cluster's own control plane (as static pods) on the bare-metal master.
interactions: Watches /etc/kubernetes/manifests and runs the management control plane (kube-apiserver, etcd, scheduler, controller-manager) as Static Pods.
Polls the Management Kube API Server for regular Pods assigned to this node, including guest control-plane Deployments.
Calls CRI-O over the CRI gRPC interface to manage container lifecycle and reports node status back to the management API Server.
explorationCommands:
# Check kubelet status on the master
systemctl status kubelet

# See which static pods the kubelet is running
ls /etc/kubernetes/manifests

# Inspect the master node object
oc get node <baremetal-master> -o wide

runtimeForm: systemd unit · bare metal master node
problemSolved: Runs the actual containers for the master's static pods and the guest control-plane pods scheduled here.
interactions: Receives gRPC CRI calls from the master kubelet.
Pulls control-plane images and sets up each container's namespaces and cgroups.
Invokes the OVN-Kubernetes CNI plugin to wire each container into the master node's OVS bridge.
explorationCommands:
# List running containers on the master
crictl ps

# Inspect the kube-apiserver static pod container
crictl inspect $(crictl ps --name kube-apiserver -q)

# View CRI-O logs
journalctl -u crio --no-pager | tail -50

runtimeForm: systemd unit · bare metal master node
problemSolved: The host switch every control-plane Pod and the overlay uplink plug into on the master node.
interactions: Manages the br-int OVS bridge and its port configuration on the master node.
Receives OpenFlow rules from the local OVN controller.
Handles Geneve encapsulation for control-plane traffic to the other management cluster nodes.
explorationCommands:
# Show OVS bridge topology
ovs-vsctl show

# Dump OpenFlow rules on br-int
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | head -30

# Check OVS service health
systemctl status openvswitch

problemSolved: Wires control-plane Pods into the cluster network and pushes OVN flows to the master's switch.
interactions: Runs the OVN controller that translates Southbound DB entries into OpenFlow rules on the master's br-int.
Invokes the CNI plugin to create veth pairs and assign IPs when control-plane Pods start.
Maintains the Geneve tunnel endpoints connecting the master node to the rest of the overlay.
explorationCommands:
# View OVN node logs
oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -l app=ovnkube-node --tail=50

# List OVS flows on this node
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int

# Check OVN southbound DB entries
ovn-sbctl show

problemSolved: The management cluster's own API — what the HyperShift Operator and every guest control-plane controller talk to.
interactions: Started directly by the master kubelet from a manifest in /etc/kubernetes/manifests, before any scheduler exists.
Persists all management cluster state to the Management Etcd Static Pod on the same node.
Serves the HyperShift Operator, CVO, and every controller that reconciles guest control-plane applications.
Runs as a static pod on the master, distinct from each guest's own API server which runs as a regular Pod in its HCP namespace.
explorationCommands:
# Confirm the API server static pod is running on the master
oc get pods -n openshift-kube-apiserver -l apiserver=true -o wide

# Check API server health locally on the node
curl -k https://localhost:6443/healthz

# View the static pod manifest
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-apiserver-pod.yaml | head -40

problemSolved: Where infrastructure intent lives: HostedCluster, NodePool and every guest control-plane definition are records here, not processes.
interactions: Receives reads and writes exclusively from the Management Kube API Server on the same node.
Persists the HostedCluster and NodePool intent objects that the HyperShift Operator reconciles.
Replicates writes across the master nodes' etcd members via the Raft consensus protocol.
Backed up and health-checked by the management cluster's cluster-etcd-operator.
Runs as a static pod on the master; each guest cluster keeps its own separate etcd inside its HCP namespace.
explorationCommands:
# Check management etcd health
oc exec -n openshift-etcd etcd-<master> -- etcdctl endpoint health

# List etcd members
oc exec -n openshift-etcd etcd-<master> -- etcdctl member list -w table

# View the static pod manifest
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/etcd-pod.yaml | head -40

problemSolved: Runs the control loops that keep the management cluster — including the guest control-plane Deployments — at desired state.
interactions: Watches the Management Kube API Server for resource events.
Scales the guest control-plane Deployments (Guest API Server, OAuth, etc.) created by the HyperShift Operator.
Manages node lifecycle and writes status updates back to the management API Server.
explorationCommands:
# Check the controller-manager static pod
oc get pods -n openshift-kube-controller-manager -l kube-controller-manager=true

# View controller leases
oc get lease -n kube-system

# View the static pod manifest
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-controller-manager-pod.yaml | head -40

problemSolved: Places management-cluster Pods — guest control-plane and KubeVirt launcher Pods — onto bare-metal nodes.
interactions: Watches the Management Kube API Server for Pods with no node assignment.
Evaluates bare metal node capacity, taints, tolerations, and affinity rules.
Writes Binding objects back to the API Server to place guest control-plane and KubeVirt Pods onto nodes.
explorationCommands:
# Check the scheduler static pod
oc get pods -n openshift-kube-scheduler -l app=openshift-kube-scheduler

# Inspect scheduling decisions for a control-plane pod
oc describe pod <pod> -n <hcp-namespace> | grep -A5 Events

# View the static pod manifest
cat /etc/kubernetes/manifests/kube-scheduler-pod.yaml | head -40

runtimeForm: systemd unit · bare metal worker node
problemSolved: The agent that runs Pods on the bare-metal worker — including the KubeVirt launcher that hosts a guest VM.
interactions: Polls the Bare Metal API Server for PodSpecs assigned to this node.
Calls CRI-O via the CRI gRPC interface to manage container lifecycle.
Reports node and Pod resource usage back to the Bare Metal API Server.
explorationCommands:
# Check kubelet status
systemctl status kubelet

# View kubelet logs
journalctl -u kubelet -f --no-pager | tail -50

# Check node conditions
oc describe node <baremetal-worker-node>

runtimeForm: systemd unit · bare metal worker node
problemSolved: Runs the host-side containers, including the launcher container that wraps a guest virtual machine.
interactions: Receives gRPC CRI calls from the host Kubelet.
Pulls container images from the registry and creates container namespaces.
Invokes the CNI plugin to connect containers to the OVS bridge.
explorationCommands:
# List running containers
crictl ps

# Inspect the KubeVirt launcher container
crictl inspect $(crictl ps --name launcher | awk 'NR>1{print $1}')

# View CRI-O logs
journalctl -u crio --no-pager | tail -50

runtimeForm: systemd unit · bare metal worker node
problemSolved: The host switch that joins Pod veths, the overlay uplink, and the KubeVirt VM tap into one bridge.
interactions: Manages the br-int OVS bridge and its port configuration.
Receives OpenFlow rules from the local OVN controller.
Handles Geneve encapsulation for inter-node overlay traffic.
Connects the KubeVirt VM's tap interface to the overlay network.
explorationCommands:
# Show OVS bridge topology
ovs-vsctl show

# Dump OpenFlow rules
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | head -30

# Check OVS service health
systemctl status openvswitch

problemSolved: Wires worker-node Pods into the network and syncs OVN flows to the host switch.
interactions: Runs the OVN controller that translates Southbound DB entries to OpenFlow rules.
Invokes the CNI plugin to create veth pairs and assign IPs when Pods start.
Manages the Geneve tunnel endpoints for cross-node traffic.
explorationCommands:
# View OVN node logs
oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes -l app=ovnkube-node --tail=50

# List OVS flows on this node
ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int

# Check OVN SB entries for this node
ovn-sbctl show

problemSolved: The node agent that actually boots a VirtualMachineInstance into a running VM on its node.
interactions: Watches the management API Server for VirtualMachineInstances assigned to this node.
Signals the virt-launcher Pod (created by virt-controller) to define and boot its qemu-kvm domain via libvirt, then manages that VM's lifecycle on the node.
Reports VMI phase and node-level virtualization health back to the API Server.
Runs as a DaemonSet Pod on every bare-metal node that can host VMs.
explorationCommands:
# Find virt-handler on the worker nodes
oc get pods -n openshift-cnv -l kubevirt.io=virt-handler -o wide

# View virt-handler logs for this node
oc logs -n openshift-cnv <virt-handler-pod> --tail=50

# List the VMIs it is managing
oc get vmi -A -o wide

problemSolved: The Pod that wraps one VM, so KubeVirt can manage a qemu-kvm guest like any other Kubernetes application.
interactions: Spawns and supervises the qemu-kvm process for the Guest Worker Node VM.

Creates a tap interface (tap0) backing the guest's virtio NIC; under KubeVirt's default masquerade binding it sits on a pod-local bridge (k6t-eth0) with NAT, while the launcher Pod's own eth0 veth is what attaches to the host OVS bridge.
Exposes virtio device interfaces (virtio-net, virtio-blk) to the guest OS.
explorationCommands:
# Find the launcher pod
oc get pods -n <hcp-namespace> -l kubevirt.io=virt-launcher

# Inspect qemu process
oc exec -n <hcp-namespace> <launcher-pod> -- ps aux | grep qemu

# View virtual NIC config
oc exec -n <hcp-namespace> <launcher-pod> -- ip link show tap0

problemSolved: A full RHCOS VM that acts as a guest cluster worker node — where application Pods actually run.
interactions: Registers with the Guest API Server as a standard Kubernetes Node.
Runs guest kubelet, CRI-O, and OVN-Kubernetes node DaemonSet inside the VM.
Network traffic enters and exits through the tap0 virtual NIC managed by the KubeVirt Launcher.
Runs a complete Kubernetes node stack (kubelet, CRI-O, OVS) inside the VM.
explorationCommands:
# SSH into the guest worker node (via virtctl)
virtctl ssh core@<vmi-name> -n <hcp-namespace>

# Check node status from guest cluster perspective
oc get nodes --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# View qemu-kvm process on host
oc exec -n <hcp-namespace> <launcher-pod> -- ps aux | grep qemu

runtimeForm: systemd unit · guest worker node (in VM)
problemSolved: The node agent inside the worker VM that pulls and runs the guest cluster's application Pods.
interactions: Maintains an outbound watch on the exposed Guest API Server endpoint — the kubelet pulls its application; the API Server does not push to it through Konnectivity.
Calls guest CRI-O to manage container lifecycle for application Pods.
Reports node resource usage and Pod status back to the Guest API Server.
explorationCommands:
# Check kubelet inside the VM
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- systemctl status kubelet

# View guest kubelet logs
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- journalctl -u kubelet --no-pager | tail -50

runtimeForm: systemd unit · guest worker node (in VM)
problemSolved: Runs the actual application containers inside the guest worker VM.
interactions: Receives gRPC CRI calls from the guest Kubelet.
Invokes the CNI plugin to connect containers to the guest OVS bridge.
Sets up cgroup v2 hierarchies for application Pod resource isolation.
explorationCommands:
# List containers inside the guest VM
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- crictl ps

# Inspect a container
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- crictl inspect <container_id>

# View CRI-O logs in guest
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- journalctl -u crio --no-pager | tail -50

runtimeForm: systemd unit · guest worker node (in VM)
problemSolved: The in-VM switch that all guest application Pods plug into.
interactions: Manages the in-VM br-int OVS bridge for guest Pod networking.
Receives OpenFlow rules from the guest OVN-Kubernetes node DaemonSet.
Traffic exits the VM through the virtio-net interface to the host tap0 device.
explorationCommands:
# Show guest OVS topology
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- ovs-vsctl show

# Dump guest OpenFlow rules
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | head -30

problemSolved: Wires guest application Pods into the network and syncs OVN flows inside the VM.
interactions: Runs the OVN controller that programs guest OVS flows.
Invokes CNI to create veth pairs for application Pods inside the VM.
Maintains Geneve tunnel configuration for cross-node (cross-VM) traffic.
explorationCommands:
# View OVN guest node logs
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- oc logs -n openshift-ovn-kubernetes ovnkube-node-<id>

# Check guest OVN southbound DB
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- ovn-sbctl show

problemSolved: The node-side tunnel that lets the guest API server reach this node's kubelet for exec, logs, and port-forward.
interactions: Opens a persistent TLS connection to the Konnectivity Server in the bare metal cluster.
Proxies API Server → kubelet traffic through the established tunnel.
Required for 'oc exec', 'oc logs', and 'oc port-forward' to work on guest Pods.
explorationCommands:
# Check konnectivity agent inside VM
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- oc get pods -n kube-system -l app=konnectivity-agent

# Verify tunnel connectivity
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- curl -k https://<konnectivity-server>:8091/healthz

problemSolved: Resolves cluster service names for Pods on this node, with local caching to cut lookup latency.
interactions: Configured as the cluster DNS server for all containers via the kubelet's clusterDNS setting.
Answers cluster-local queries (*.svc.cluster.local) from the guest cluster's own Service/Endpoint records and forwards external names to the upstream resolvers configured on the node.
Caches resolved records to reduce lookup latency for busy applications.
explorationCommands:
# Check node-level CoreDNS
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- oc get pods -n openshift-dns -l dns.operator.openshift.io/daemonset-dns=default

# Test DNS from a application pod
oc exec <pod> -n <ns> -- nslookup kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local

problemSolved: The guest cluster's own front door for application (*.apps) traffic — separate from the control-plane proxy.
interactions: Watches Route objects in the guest cluster via the Guest API Server.

Receives *.apps application traffic via the guest's router-default LoadBalancer, after it enters the VM from the infra-side Apps Ingress LoadBalancer — NOT through the Shared Ingress Proxy, which fronts the control-plane API only.
Terminates TLS and forwards each request to the matching Service (e.g. the Front-End Service) inside the guest cluster.
explorationCommands:
# Check guest ingress router
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- oc get pods -n openshift-ingress

# View guest routes
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- oc get route -A

# Inspect HAProxy config
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- oc exec -n openshift-ingress <router-pod> -- cat /var/lib/haproxy/conf/haproxy.config | head -40

linuxPrimitive: router-default LB → kubevirt CCM mirror → OVN LB flows
problemSolved: The guest-side LoadBalancer that fronts the in-VM ingress router for *.apps traffic.
interactions: Selects the guest Ingress Router Pods and exposes them behind the router-default external IP.
Its external IP is assigned and wired to the infra-side Apps Ingress LoadBalancer by the kubevirt cloud provider (CCM), not by a MetalLB speaker inside the guest.
Traffic to the VIP is DNATed by guest OVN load-balancer flows to a healthy router Pod endpoint.
explorationCommands:
# View the router-default LoadBalancer service and its external IP
oc get svc router-default -n openshift-ingress -o wide --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Confirm MetalLB assigned the address from a pool
oc get ipaddresspool -n metallb-system --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# See the speaker announcing the VIP
oc logs -n metallb-system -l component=speaker --tail=50 --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig> | grep announcing

problemSolved: The user-facing application — the terminal destination of the whole external traffic flow.
interactions: Listens on a private Pod IP address within the guest cluster network.
Receives traffic from the Guest Ingress Router via the in-VM OVS bridge.
May call the Back-End Application Pod via east-west Service traffic within the guest cluster.
explorationCommands:
# Check application pods
oc get pods -n e-commerce-prod -l app=frontend

# View app logs
oc logs -n e-commerce-prod deploy/frontend --tail=50

# Exec into the container
oc exec -it deploy/frontend -n e-commerce-prod -- /bin/sh

# Check listening ports
oc exec deploy/frontend -n e-commerce-prod -- ss -tlnp

problemSolved: Gives the front-end Pods one stable virtual IP so clients never chase churning Pod addresses.
interactions: Selects the frontend Pods by label and tracks their ready endpoints via the EndpointSlice controller.
The Guest Ingress Router resolves the Service and forwards inbound requests to it.
The ClusterIP is virtual — OVN-Kubernetes programs load-balancer flows that DNAT it to a backing Pod IP.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect the ClusterIP service
oc get svc frontend -n e-commerce-prod -o wide

# List the endpoints it currently routes to
oc get endpointslices -n e-commerce-prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=frontend

# Show the OVN load-balancer entry backing the ClusterIP
ovn-nbctl lb-list | grep <cluster-ip>

problemSolved: The application's data and API tier, called east-west by the front end.
interactions: Fronted by the Back-End ClusterIP Service, which the Front-End Application consumes for east-west API calls.
Connects to persistent storage and external databases.
Communicates over the in-VM guest OVS bridge via the OVN virtual fabric.
explorationCommands:
# Check backend pods
oc get pods -n e-commerce-prod -l app=backend

# View backend logs
oc logs -n e-commerce-prod deploy/backend --tail=50

# Check service endpoints
oc get endpoints backend-svc -n e-commerce-prod

problemSolved: Gives the back-end Pods a stable virtual IP so back-end scaling and rollouts stay invisible to the front end.
interactions: Selects the backend Pods by label and publishes their ready endpoints.
Consumed east-west by the Front-End Application via the Service DNS name (backend.e-commerce-prod.svc).
The ClusterIP is realized as OVN load-balancer flows that DNAT to a backing Pod IP on the guest OVS fabric.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect the ClusterIP service
oc get svc backend -n e-commerce-prod -o wide

# Check the endpoints behind the service
oc get endpoints backend -n e-commerce-prod

# Resolve the service DNS from the frontend pod
oc exec deploy/frontend -n e-commerce-prod -- nslookup backend.e-commerce-prod.svc.cluster.local

linuxPrimitive: OVN ACL + address set → OVS allow/drop flows
problemSolved: Locks down east-west traffic: only the front end may reach the back end, everything else is denied.
interactions: Selects the Back-End Application Pods via podSelector and gates their ingress to the Front-End Pods' address set on the backend port.
Watched by the OVN-Kubernetes Master, which translates it into ACLs and address sets in the OVN Northbound DB.
Enforced in the data plane as allow/drop OpenFlow rules on the guest Open vSwitch br-int — non-matching traffic is dropped before it reaches the backend veth.
Unlike a plain config object it has a real datapath — OVN-Kubernetes compiles it into ACLs enforced as allow/drop flows on the guest br-int, which earns it a card on the canvas.
explorationCommands:
# List NetworkPolicies in the namespace
oc get networkpolicy -n e-commerce-prod

# Inspect the policy rules
oc get networkpolicy backend-allow-frontend -n e-commerce-prod -o yaml

# Show the OVN ACLs the policy compiled into
ovn-nbctl acl-list <port-group>

problemSolved: Gives each application Pod its own private network — IP, routes, and firewall — isolated from every other Pod.
interactions: Attaches to a guest-side veth pair managed by the OVN-Kubernetes Guest Node DaemonSet.
Provisioned and configured by the guest CRI-O runtime via CNI instructions.
explorationCommands:
# Find the target host PID of the container
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- crictl inspect <container_id> | grep pid

# Enter the isolated network namespace
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- nsenter -t <PID> -n ip addr show

problemSolved: Caps each container's CPU, memory, and I/O so one runaway Pod can't starve the node.
interactions: Hierarchy created by guest CRI-O/runc when the container starts inside the VM.
Guest kubelet monitors cgroup usage and reports resource consumption.
OOM killer is triggered when a container exceeds its memory limit.
explorationCommands:
# Find cgroup path for a container
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- crictl inspect <container_id> | grep cgroupsPath

# View memory limit
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<cgroup_path>/memory.max

# View CPU quota
virtctl ssh core@<vmi> -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/<cgroup_path>/cpu.max

runtimeForm: Linux process · PID 1 in netns (in VM)
linuxPrimitive: execve() under PID 1 in VM netns
problemSolved: The application process itself (PID 1) — the leaf where the entire HCP ownership chain finally runs.
interactions: Runs inside the intersection of a Network Namespace, cgroup slice, and PID namespace — all inside the Guest VM.
Receives inbound socket connections on its private Pod IP address.
Writes logs to stdout/stderr captured by the guest container runtime.
explorationCommands:
# Exec into the container
oc exec -it <pod-name> -n <namespace> -- /bin/sh

# View the process tree
oc exec <pod-name> -n <namespace> -- ps aux

# Check listening ports
oc exec <pod-name> -n <namespace> -- ss -tlnp

problemSolved: The per-guest control-plane spec the Control Plane Operator reconciles into real Deployments.
interactions: Created by the HyperShift Operator from the HostedCluster, in the guest's HCP namespace on the management API Server.
Reconciled by the Control Plane Operator, which renders it into the guest control-plane Deployments and StatefulSets.
Surfaces per-component control-plane status and the rolled-out release version.
A desired-state record in the management etcd, not a running process.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect the HostedControlPlane
oc get hostedcontrolplane -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

# Watch its rollout conditions
oc get hostedcontrolplane -n <hcp-namespace> -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.conditions}'

problemSolved: The root of the machine ownership tree that ultimately provisions this hosted cluster's worker VMs.
interactions: Authored by the HyperShift Operator's NodePool controller in the HCP namespace.
Reconciled by the Cluster API Manager as the parent of the MachineDeployment / MachineSet / Machine tree.
References the KubeVirt infrastructure provider that backs this cluster's machines.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect the CAPI Cluster object
oc get cluster.cluster.x-k8s.io -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

# List the Machines it owns
oc get machines.cluster.x-k8s.io -n <hcp-namespace>

problemSolved: Manages rolling upgrades of the guest worker pool, the way a Deployment does for Pods.
interactions: Rendered by the HyperShift NodePool controller from the NodePool's replica count and release.
Reconciled by the Cluster API Manager, which creates and scales the backing MachineSet.
Drives rolling upgrades by replacing MachineSets rather than mutating Machines in place.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect the MachineDeployment
oc get machinedeployment -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

# Check its rollout status
oc get machinedeployment -n <hcp-namespace>

problemSolved: Guarantees a stable count of identical guest worker Machines, like a ReplicaSet for nodes.
interactions: Owned by the MachineDeployment, which sets its replica count during rollouts.
Reconciled by the Cluster API Manager, which creates or deletes Machine objects to match desired replicas.
Reports the number of ready Machines back up to the MachineDeployment.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect the MachineSet
oc get machineset.cluster.x-k8s.io -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

# List the Machines it owns
oc get machines.cluster.x-k8s.io -n <hcp-namespace>

problemSolved: The provider-agnostic intent for a single guest worker node.
interactions: Created by its owning MachineSet to represent one desired guest worker node.
Paired by the Cluster API Manager with a KubevirtMachine that supplies the real infrastructure.
Becomes Running once the backing VirtualMachineInstance registers as a guest cluster Node.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect a Machine
oc get machine.cluster.x-k8s.io -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

# See its phase (Provisioning / Running / Deleting)
oc get machines.cluster.x-k8s.io -n <hcp-namespace> -o wide

problemSolved: The KubeVirt-specific half of a Machine that turns generic node intent into a real VM.
interactions: Created alongside each Machine as its infrastructure reference.
Reconciled by the CAPI Provider (KubeVirt), which creates the backing KubeVirt VirtualMachine.
Reports the VM's node addresses and ready state back to its paired Machine.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect a KubevirtMachine
oc get kubevirtmachine -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

# Map it to its VirtualMachine
oc get vm -n <hcp-namespace>

problemSolved: The desired-state record of a guest worker VM that KubeVirt runs as a live VirtualMachineInstance.
interactions: Created by the CAPI Provider (KubeVirt) from a KubevirtMachine.
Reconciled by KubeVirt's virt-controller into a running VirtualMachineInstance when its runStrategy says so.
Spec changes (CPU, memory, disks) re-roll the VMI rather than mutating the live guest in place.
The VM is the intent; the VirtualMachineInstance shown on the canvas is its running realisation.
explorationCommands:
# Inspect the VirtualMachine
oc get vm -n <hcp-namespace> -o yaml

# Confirm the running VMI it produced
oc get vmi -n <hcp-namespace> -o wide

problemSolved: Declares the OpenShift version the guest cluster should be running.
interactions: Read by the Cluster Version Operator to determine the guest cluster's target release.
Updated by an admin (oc adm upgrade) to request an upgrade to a new channel or version.
Surfaces the overall update progress and history in its status.
explorationCommands:
# View the ClusterVersion and upgrade status
oc get clusterversion --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect available updates
oc adm upgrade --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: Each guest operator's health report — and the gate that blocks upgrades when something is degraded.
interactions: Written by each guest second-level operator to publish its Available / Progressing / Degraded state.
Watched by the Cluster Version Operator, which blocks upgrades while any operator is Degraded.
Read by admins to triage which guest cluster component is unhealthy.
explorationCommands:
# List ClusterOperators and their conditions
oc get clusteroperators --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect one operator's conditions
oc get clusteroperator ingress -o yaml --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: Declares the public hostname and TLS policy that exposes a guest Service to the outside world.
interactions: Authored by the app owner to publish the Front-End Service under a public hostname.
Watched by the Guest Ingress Router, which compiles it into HAProxy frontend/backend config.
References a target Service and the TLS termination policy (edge / passthrough / reencrypt).
Pure config in the guest etcd with no process of its own — which is why it lives in the store, not on the canvas.
explorationCommands:
# List Routes in the namespace
oc get route -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect a Route's host and TLS
oc get route frontend -n e-commerce-prod -o yaml --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: Declares the desired replicas and Pod template for each app tier — the source the application Pods are reconciled from.
interactions: Authored by the app owner to declare the desired replicas and container image for each tier.
Reconciled by the guest Deployment controller into a ReplicaSet on every spec change.
Drives rolling updates by creating a new ReplicaSet and scaling the old one to zero.
explorationCommands:
# List Deployments in the namespace
oc get deploy -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect the front-end Deployment
oc get deploy frontend -n e-commerce-prod -o yaml --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: Guarantees the application Pods stay at their desired count, recreating any that are lost.
interactions: Created and owned by a Deployment, which sets its replica count during rollouts.
Reconciled by the guest ReplicaSet controller, which creates or deletes Pods to match desired replicas.
Owns the application Pods via ownerReferences so they are garbage-collected with it.
explorationCommands:
# List ReplicaSets in the namespace
oc get rs -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# See which Pods a ReplicaSet owns
oc get pods -n e-commerce-prod -l app=frontend -o wide --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

linuxPrimitive: etcd record (guest etcd, encrypted at rest)
problemSolved: Holds the app's sensitive config so credentials live outside the container image.
interactions: Referenced by the application Pod specs as volume mounts or environment variables.
Projected by the guest kubelet into the Pod as an in-memory tmpfs mount, not a disk file.
Persisted in the guest etcd — encrypted at rest, since HyperShift enables etcd Secret encryption by default (in vanilla Kubernetes this is opt-in); access is gated by RBAC on the Secret resource.
explorationCommands:
# List Secrets in the namespace
oc get secret -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Decode a Secret value
oc get secret backend-db-credentials -n e-commerce-prod -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig> | base64 -d

problemSolved: Holds the app's non-sensitive config, decoupling settings from the container image.
interactions: Referenced by the application Pod specs as mounted volumes or envFrom sources.
Projected into the Pod by the guest kubelet as a tmpfs mount at container start.
Updated independently of the image; a rollout or reload picks up the new values.
explorationCommands:
# List ConfigMaps in the namespace
oc get configmap -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect a ConfigMap's data
oc get configmap frontend-app-config -n e-commerce-prod -o yaml --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: A application's request for storage — bound to a volume and mounted into its Pod.
interactions: Authored alongside the application to request a size and storage class.
Bound by the guest control plane to a matching PersistentVolume.
Triggers the guest kubelet to attach and mount the backing block device into the Pod.
explorationCommands:
# List PVCs in the namespace
oc get pvc -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# See which PV a claim is bound to
oc get pvc pvc-backend-data -n e-commerce-prod -o jsonpath='{.spec.volumeName}' --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: The actual storage asset a claim binds to, surfacing as a block device inside the guest VM.
interactions: Provisioned (dynamically by a CSI driver, or statically by an admin) to satisfy a PVC.
Bound one-to-one to a PersistentVolumeClaim once their size and class match.
Realised inside the guest VM as a block device (/dev/vdb, /dev/vdc) mounted by the kubelet.
explorationCommands:
# List PersistentVolumes (cluster-scoped)
oc get pv --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect a PV's source and claim binding
oc get pv pv-block-data -o yaml --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: The live list of ready Pod IPs behind a Service — what OVN reads to load-balance a ClusterIP to a real Pod.
interactions: Maintained by the guest EndpointSlice controller as Pods behind a Service become ready or unready.
Lists the current ready Pod IPs and ports for its owning Service.
Read by OVN-Kubernetes to program the ClusterIP load-balancer (DNAT) flows.
explorationCommands:
# List EndpointSlices for a Service
oc get endpointslices -n e-commerce-prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=frontend --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect the ready endpoints
oc get endpointslices -n e-commerce-prod -o yaml --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: Rolls out Deployments by creating and scaling the ReplicaSets behind them — including the guest control-plane Deployments the HyperShift Operator stamps out.
interactions: Watches the Management Kube API Server for Deployment objects and the ReplicaSets they own.
Creates a new ReplicaSet on each pod-template change and scales the old one down to roll the update out.
Reconciles the guest control-plane Deployments (Guest API Server, OAuth, etc.) toward their desired replica count.
explorationCommands:
# Watch Deployments roll out
oc get deploy -A -w

# Inspect a Deployment's managed ReplicaSets
oc describe deploy <name> -n <ns>

problemSolved: Keeps the actual number of Pods for each ReplicaSet equal to its desired replica count, creating or deleting Pods to match.
interactions: Watches ReplicaSets and the Pods they own on the management API Server.
Creates Pods when actual is below desired and deletes surplus Pods when it is above.
Adopts matching orphan Pods via their ownerReferences.
explorationCommands:
# List ReplicaSets and their ready counts
oc get rs -A

# See which Pods a ReplicaSet owns
oc get pods -n <ns> -l <selector> -o wide

problemSolved: Watches node heartbeats and taints or evicts workloads from bare-metal nodes that stop reporting healthy.
interactions: Monitors the Lease and status heartbeats each bare-metal kubelet posts to the management API Server.
Applies NoExecute / NoSchedule taints when a node goes NotReady.
Triggers eviction of Pods from a node that stays unreachable past the grace period.
explorationCommands:
# Check node readiness and taints
oc get nodes -o wide

# Inspect node conditions
oc describe node <node> | grep -A10 Conditions

problemSolved: Drives namespace teardown — once a Namespace is marked for deletion it purges every object inside before the namespace itself is removed.
interactions: Watches Namespaces on the management API Server for a deletionTimestamp.
Deletes all resources in the namespace, then clears the kubernetes finalizer.
Blocks final removal until every contained object is gone.
explorationCommands:
# Watch namespaces and their phase
oc get ns

# Inspect a stuck namespace's finalizers
oc get ns <name> -o jsonpath='{.spec.finalizers}'

problemSolved: Ensures every namespace has a default ServiceAccount so the Pods scheduled into it have an identity to authenticate with.
interactions: Watches Namespaces and creates the default ServiceAccount in each.
Works alongside the token controller to provision the API credentials Pods mount.
Backs the identities the guest control-plane Pods run as.
explorationCommands:
# List ServiceAccounts in a namespace
oc get sa -n <ns>

# Inspect the default ServiceAccount
oc get sa default -n <ns> -o yaml

problemSolved: Binds PersistentVolumeClaims to suitable PersistentVolumes and drives dynamic provisioning of new ones.
interactions: Watches PVCs and PVs on the management API Server.
Matches a pending claim to an available volume and binds the pair, or triggers a provisioner.
Reclaims released volumes according to their reclaim policy.
explorationCommands:

oc get pvc -A

# Inspect PersistentVolume bind status
oc get pv

problemSolved: Watches guest worker node heartbeats and taints or evicts workloads from VMI nodes that stop reporting healthy.
interactions: Monitors the Lease heartbeats each guest kubelet posts to the Guest API Server.
Taints a guest node NotReady when its KubeVirt VMI stops reporting.
Evicts guest Pods from a node that stays unreachable past the grace period.

oc get nodes -o wide --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect guest node conditions
oc describe node <node> --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig> | grep -A10 Conditions

problemSolved: Rolls out the guest cluster's application Deployments (the e-commerce front-end / back-end) by managing the ReplicaSets behind them.
interactions: Watches Deployments on the Guest API Server.
Creates a new ReplicaSet on each pod-template change and scales the old one down.
Keeps the e-commerce application Deployments at their desired replica count.
explorationCommands:
# Watch application Deployments
oc get deploy -n e-commerce-prod -w --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect rollout status
oc rollout status deploy/frontend -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: Keeps the actual number of application Pods equal to each ReplicaSet's desired replica count, creating or deleting Pods to match.
interactions: Watches ReplicaSets and the Pods they own on the Guest API Server.
Creates Pods when actual is below desired and deletes surplus Pods when it is above.

explorationCommands:
# List ReplicaSets and their ready counts
oc get rs -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# See which Pods a ReplicaSet owns

problemSolved: Keeps each Service's EndpointSlice in sync with the live, ready Pod IPs behind it — the list OVN reads to load-balance a ClusterIP to a real Pod.
interactions: Watches Services, Pods, and their readiness on the Guest API Server.
Writes ready Pod IPs into the Service's EndpointSlice as Pods come and go.
Drives the data the guest OVN-Kubernetes reads to DNAT a ClusterIP onto a live Pod.
explorationCommands:
# List EndpointSlices for a Service
oc get endpointslices -n e-commerce-prod -l kubernetes.io/service-name=frontend --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect the ready endpoints
oc get endpointslices -n e-commerce-prod -o yaml --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: Ensures every guest namespace has a default ServiceAccount so the application Pods scheduled into it have an identity to authenticate with.
interactions: Watches guest Namespaces and creates the default ServiceAccount in each.
Works alongside the token controller to provision the API credentials guest Pods mount.
Backs the identities the e-commerce application Pods run as.
explorationCommands:
# List ServiceAccounts in a guest namespace
oc get sa -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect the default ServiceAccount
oc get sa default -n e-commerce-prod -o yaml --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

problemSolved: Binds the guest application PersistentVolumeClaims to suitable PersistentVolumes and drives dynamic provisioning of new ones.
interactions: Watches PVCs and PVs on the Guest API Server.
Matches a pending claim to an available volume and binds the pair, or triggers a provisioner.
Reclaims released volumes according to their reclaim policy.
explorationCommands:
# List PVCs and their bound volumes
oc get pvc -n e-commerce-prod --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>

# Inspect PersistentVolume bind status
oc get pv --kubeconfig <guest-kubeconfig>
